attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: A faithful restatement of a present-tense availability observation as of the post date.

contract.note: Reading 'arrived' as ordinary customer availability is a fair, ordinary reading. The date rule is strict: it treats later launch announcements as context only and asks for explicit evidence of the state on the target date.

evidence.note: Oct 1, 2024 report of no new models at DevDay and Sora still pending. It is consistent with the claim but predates the Oct 20 target date and does not cover GPT-5 explicitly.
OpenAI's own Dec 2024 Sora launch announcement. Under the contract's date rule, a later launch event is context only.
OpenAI's own Aug 2025 GPT-5 introduction. It is a later launch event, so context only under the contract.

reviews.rationale: Everything in the packet is consistent with neither product being publicly available on Oct 20, 2024, and nothing contradicts that. But the contract asks for a dated record of the state on the target date and treats later launches as context. The only near-date item is from Oct 1 and does not address GPT-5 directly. The packet itself reports this gap, so under the contract's own rules the outcome is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: Faithful. It correctly drops 'interesting' as opinion. 'Far from a general solution' is partly evaluative.

contract.note: Reading 'expensive to operate' as the cost of serving the model is ordinary, and customer prices still count as indirect evidence. The speaker gave no threshold for 'expensive' or for 'general solution', so the result depends on the evaluator's interpretation.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own statement that GPT-4o is more capable for many common cases. This supports the limitations part. It is a company disclosure.
OpenAI's own preference evaluation finds o1-preview not well suited to all use cases. This supports uneven, non-general performance.
OpenAI says, qualitatively, that such models can be expensive and slow. This is not a matched disclosure of what it costs OpenAI to run the model.
METR found many of the agent failures it sampled may be spurious. This cautions against treating them as hard capability limits. It does not rebut the claim of limits on ordinary tasks.

reviews.rationale: OpenAI's own disclosures (e8, e9) support the limitations part. There is no matched evidence of what it cost OpenAI to run the model; e10 is only qualitative. The claim joins both parts, so the expense part keeps it from being settled, and nothing contradicts either part.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: Keeps 'everyone's expectations' and 'hard to call'. The smoke-and-mirrors conclusion is rhetorical. The factual core is that products shipped and that expectations went unmet.

contract.note: Keeping the unmet-expectations part is fair to the speaker. But the speaker named no expectations and no degree of shortfall, so how 'by a longshot' is read decides the result.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own disclosure shows GPT-4o was available to customers in May 2024. This supports the 'they ship' part.
OpenAI's own disclosure of an Oct 2024 public beta for paid developers. This supports shipping before the post.
OpenAI's own post, reproduced by Thread Reader App, about delaying the voice mode rollout. It shows one specific shortfall, not one 'by a longshot' against broad expectations.

reviews.rationale: The shipping and customer-access part is supported by e12 and e13. For unmet expectations, the packet shows only one modest delay (e14). That does not establish a substantial shortfall against identifiable expectations, and nothing contradicts it either. The smoke-and-mirrors conclusion is rhetoric and is not scored on its own, so the claim as a whole is unresolved.
